title: Proposed Tax Credit Restrictions Would Cost Dreamer Families $4,560 a Year, Hit 90,000 Citizen Children
excerpt: New IRS regulations would strip Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit access from DACA recipients and other lawfully present immigrants, with more than half of those affected being U.S. citizens.
body:
• Proposed IRS regulations would strip Earned Income Tax Credit and Additional Child Tax Credit access from DACA recipients, Temporary Protected Status holders, and other lawfully present immigrants
  • An ITEP analysis found 158,000 people in DACA households would lose an average of $4,560 per year, with 90,000 U.S. citizen children among those harmed
  • The regulations would also require all 49 million families claiming these credits to report citizenship status on tax returns for the first time

The U.S. Treasury Department and Internal Revenue Service have proposed regulations that would bar DACA recipients and other lawfully present immigrants from claiming key federal tax credits, a move that a new analysis says would financially harm 158,000 people — more than half of them U.S. citizens — while requiring tens of millions of American families to disclose their citizenship status to the IRS for the first time.

The proposed rules, released in August 2026, would reclassify the refundable portions of four federal tax credits as "federal public benefits" under the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (PRWORA). The credits affected are the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC), American Opportunity Tax Credit, and Adoption Tax Credit.

Who Would Be Hit

According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP), the restrictions would affect immigrants who are legally authorized to work in the United States and pay taxes with valid Social Security numbers but do not meet the narrow legal definition of a "qualified alien" under the 1996 welfare law. That includes DACA recipients — often called Dreamers — people with Temporary Protected Status, pending asylum applicants, and many visa holders.

ITEP's updated analysis, focused specifically on the DACA recipient population, found that 158,000 people who are either DACA recipients or live and file taxes with them would be harmed. The average affected family would lose $4,560 in credits per year — 13 percent of their annual income of roughly $35,000.

"Among families with DACA recipients, more than half of the people who would be harmed are U.S. citizens, and most of those individuals are children."

— ITEP analysis

U.S. Citizen Children Bear the Brunt

The analysis found that 90,000 U.S. citizen children would lose tax credit support, accounting for 57 percent of all affected individuals. The average DACA recipient affected by the proposal has lived in the United States for over 28 years and was brought to the country at about age 7.

Because the EITC and ACTC both require earned income as a condition of eligibility, only working families who file tax returns would be affected — not those outside the tax system. The financial impact would be compounded in as many as 30 of the 32 states with their own Earned Income Tax Credits, which piggyback on federal eligibility rules.

Under a married-filing-jointly provision, only one spouse needs to meet the "qualified alien" requirement for the household to retain benefits. This protects some mixed-status couples, but offers no relief to unmarried filers or couples where neither partner qualifies.

A Citizenship Question on Tax Returns

To enforce the new rules, the IRS said it plans to require all filers who claim any of the four credits — approximately 49 million families, according to ITEP — to report their citizenship status directly on their tax return. Tax policy researchers at the Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center noted this would mark the first time the IRS has asked filers to disclose citizenship on a return.

The regulations build on restrictions Congress already enacted in H.R. 1 of 2025, which barred families from claiming the Child Tax Credit unless at least one parent has a Social Security number. That change alone cut off an estimated 2.7 million American citizen children from the credit, according to the Center for the Study of Social Policy.

A Reversal From Trump's Own First Term

The proposal marks a reversal from the position taken during the first Trump administration, when the Department of Homeland Security articulated multiple reasons that tax credits should not be classified as federal public benefits under PRWORA, citing complexities with mixed-status families and the structure of the tax system.

The White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs began reviewing the proposed rules in July 2026, according to Bloomberg Tax, following a Justice Department opinion issued in November 2025 asserting that refundable tax credit portions could be treated as public benefits.

The full reach of the regulations extends well beyond DACA recipients. Treasury Department estimates suggest as many as 700,000 tax returns could be affected, implying tax credit losses for over one million people. A recent Gallup poll found that 85 percent of Americans favor giving childhood arrivals a chance to become U.S. citizens.
